papers.title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
papers.abstract: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

papers.title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
papers.abstract: Data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, and hierarchical U-shaped networks, which resemble the structure of classical Geometric Multigrid (GMG) methods, have become prevalent designs. Modern surrogates built on these designs achieve competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers; however, accurate prediction of complex flows remains challenging, and no existing architecture leads across them. In such networks, the multigrid analogy mainly concerns the multi-resolution topology, while their components largely follow common vision practice. To address this, this study introduces SUMNO, a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow fields on regular grids that spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. Parameter-free down- and upsampling stand in for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, with normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Within this macro-architecture, convolutions are used at the fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, whose window partitioning is generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis. Evaluated on unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five representative baselines, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and ranks second in the remaining two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters using 9.4 million parameters.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
papers.abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.abstract: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

papers.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

papers.title: Data-driven Correction Reduced-Order Stochastic Collocation Method for the Time-Dependent Navier-Stokes Equations
papers.abstract: We develop two hybrid data-driven Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) for the non-stationary incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations (NSEs) with random viscosity. The proposed framework combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) ROMs, spatial filtering, data-driven closure modeling, and the Stochastic Collocation Method (SCM). A key feature is the approximation of the realization-dependent closure term by the closure associated with the expected viscosity. Consequently, a single data-driven closure model constructed from the full-order solution corresponding to the expected viscosity can be reused across all realizations, thereby avoiding the expensive construction of realization-specific closure models. This leads to the Data-Driven Correction UQ ROM (DDC-UQ-ROM) and its physically constrained variant, the Constrained DDC-UQ-ROM (CDDC-UQ-ROM), in which physical constraints are imposed on the data-driven correction model. The proposed methods are evaluated for a two-dimensional (2D) flow past a circular cylinder problem with a 5D random viscosity field, considering mean Reynolds numbers $Re=100$ and $Re=500$, different correlation lengths, and both in-sample and out-of-sample parameter settings. Numerical results show that the DDC-UQ-ROM generally improves upon the standard Galerkin ROM (G-ROM), while the CDDC-UQ-ROM exhibits the most accurate and robust approximation of the benchmark energy evolution across the cases considered. The robustness and accuracy of the CDDC-UQ-ROM are further assessed through statistical error analyses of the first- and second-order energy moments, reduced-training-data experiments, and an indicative comparison of wall-clock computational costs with the full-order UQ calculations.

papers.title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
papers.abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

papers.title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking
papers.abstract: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

papers.title: Shallow water equations on n-dimensional Riemannian manifolds: a kinetic approach
papers.abstract: We develop an intrinsic kinetic moment closure for shallow-water equations on smooth manifolds of arbitrary dimension equipped with prescribed, possibly time-dependent Riemannian metrics. Hamiltonian transport on the cotangent bundle and metric-dependent momentum integration yield balance laws with hydrostatic pressure, bottom topography, a skew-adjoint force, and dissipative bottom friction. An explicit compactly supported Gibbs equilibrium satisfies the required mass, momentum, and tensor second-moment conditions. We derive the quasilinear formulation and characteristic speeds, establish the continuous mechanical-energy balance with geometric work and frictional dissipation, and obtain a weak entropy inequality for vanishing-viscosity limits under stated convergence assumptions. On the rotating sphere with a fixed round metric, the skew-adjoint force represents Coriolis effects. We construct a kinetic finite-volume scheme combining local fluxes, hydrostatic reconstruction, and geometric source terms. A second-order time integrator uses independently restricted steps at its two Euler stages. The scheme conserves discrete water volume, preserves nonnegative depth under a sufficient CFL condition, and is well balanced for lakes at rest, including wet/dry interfaces. Six-hour simulations of a localized surface disturbance over Earth topography with Manning bottom friction maintain positive depths and conserve water volume to near machine precision. Comparison with a spherical central-upwind method shows similar surface-wave propagation and gauge time series, with remaining differences in late-time local extrema.

papers.title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver
papers.abstract: We extend BK19 the semi-implicit finite-volume solver, to provide access to the quasi-geostrophic (QG) regime within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits. In order to achieve this goal, we incorporate the asymptotic framework from the continuous theory into the numerical scheme. Adopting the usual asymptotic setting for the quasi-geostrophic regime and using it directly in the numerical model, we perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations in the synoptic length and time scales in the limit of small Rossby number. In this limit, the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance, together with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint. We construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives and use it to define the vorticity in the numerical framework. An asymptotic analysis of the fully discrete scheme then yields a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation that coincides with the QG pressure Poisson equation in the continuous theory. As a result of this analysis, we introduce two additional blending switches that (i) convert the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to its QG Poisson-type equation and (ii) control whether the horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance. In combination with the existing soundproof and hydrostatic switches, the resulting algorithm can be operated in fully compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes without changing the underlying discretization. The functionality of the numerical scheme in the QG regime is then tested by two idealized vortex test cases to show how stable the vortices remain in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.

papers.title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
authors: Jun Fang (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
Ling Zou (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
Rui Hu (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division
papers.abstract: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

papers.title: TIDE: A Physically Diverse 3D Turbulence Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Turbulence is a central testbed for machine learning on physical dynamics because its governing laws are known exactly. However, most existing studies remain in 2D, while 3D turbulence has fundamentally different physics and is far more costly to simulate. Existing 3D resources also typically provide only one realization per configuration, making it difficult to distinguish learning the dynamics from fitting the statistics of a single flow. In this paper, we introduce TIDE (Turbulent Incompressible DNS Ensembles), a 256^3 DNS corpus and benchmark for 3D incompressible turbulence, with 15 configurations on eight controlled axes, independent ensembles, pressure fields, and equation-level verification. The benchmark includes five tasks, standardized learned baselines, controlled generalization splits, and physical-fidelity metrics alongside pointwise error. Across the main forecasting configurations, current learned models trained under a fixed reference recipe barely outperform persistence and still make about twice the error of a spectral solver given the true equations. Moreover, lower pointwise error can coincide with severely distorted small-scale dynamics, showing that accuracy alone does not ensure physical fidelity. Rollout stability depends on the configuration, the training seed, and how densely training samples each trajectory. Joint training across neighboring regimes does not close the transfer gaps we test, and the forced-to-decay contrast bounds a conditioning limit: an estimate of the current forcing state removes 20-41% of the error a spectral solver makes without forcing input, while history or forcing inputs help only some learned architectures. Closing these accuracy, fidelity, and conditioning gaps is the central open problem made measurable by TIDE. https://github.com/Dyloong1/TIDE-dataset-benchmark

papers.title: Boundary-layer detachment and infinite-Reynolds limit of two-dimensional wall-bounded flows
papers.abstract: Understanding boundary-layer detachment and its consequences for the infinite-Reynolds-number limit remains a major challenge in fluid mechanics. Here, direct numerical simulations of incompressible flow in a two-dimensional periodic channel with no-slip walls are used to investigate this problem. Reynolds-number-dependent initial conditions are constructed with a boundary layer of Prandtl thickness that converge in the energy norm to an analytic, stationary Euler flow, while the associated Prandtl system develops a finite-time singularity. Highly resolved simulations show boundary-layer detachment and departures from Prandtl scaling, yet provide numerical evidence that the Navier--Stokes solutions continue to converge to the Euler flow over the simulated time interval. In particular, the squared energy norm of the velocity difference and the time-averaged energy dissipation both scale approximately as $Re^{-1/2}$, consistently with established convergence criteria. Although the detached vortices become more numerous and intense as the Reynolds number increases, their characteristic size and occupied area appear to decrease. These observations suggest how boundary-layer detachment and the breakdown of the Prandtl description can coexist with convergence to a smooth Euler flow.

papers.title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes
papers.abstract: For modelling dissipative phenomena such as friction, diffusion and viscosity, the Hamiltonian framework has a key limitation: once the Casimir invariants are fixed, Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume, which rules out relaxation to equilibrium. Thus modelling dissipation requires modifying the Hamiltonian structure. Following the metriplectic (equivalently, GENERIC) approach, we add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket, here constructed from a Riemannian metric. The resulting flow conserves the energy, and optionally further invariants, while driving a chosen generalised entropy monotonically, which makes the dynamics irreversible; when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the direction in which it is driven, it acts as a Lyapunov functional. We apply this construction to ideal fluids on compact Riemannian manifolds, choosing Casimirs of the Lie-Poisson bracket as entropies. In two dimensions, dissipating enstrophy yields the already-known energy-constrained Navier-Stokes equations, which include a nonlocal term restoring energy balance. In three dimensions, where enstrophy is no longer a Casimir, we derive new irreversible models. For incompressible and compressible fluids carrying an advected scalar, dissipating potential enstrophy or higher potential-vorticity moments gives a nonlinear, anisotropic diffusion that acts to align the gradients of the scalar and of the potential vorticity. For a purely incompressible fluid, taking helicity as the entropy gives a first-order, non-smoothing dissipative term whose stationary states are Beltrami fields.

papers.title: Crystal Nucleation Driven by Microjets from Hydrodynamically Interacting Thermocavitation Bubbles
papers.abstract: Primary nucleation predominantly dictates the physicochemical, optical and mechanical properties of crystals emerging from solution. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized nucleation mechanism arising from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions using laser-induced thermocavitation bubble pairs. Under confinement, antiphase generation of two bubbles produces a micron-scale, high-speed liquid jet. Upon impact with the surrounding supersaturated liquid, this microjet generates intense localized shear, thereby inducing crystallization of the model inorganic salt, potassium permanganate. Under identical laser energies and supersaturation levels, crystallization was not observed in single-bubble experiments, in which no microjet was present. We show that the crystallization probability increases with microjet velocity. Boundary integral simulations reveal how experimental parameters such as confinement, bubble spacing, and laser energy govern microjet formation and velocity. We quantify the relationship between jet velocity and the observed enhancement in crystal nucleation kinetics by incorporating shear into the kinetic prefactor in classical nucleation theory. By combining experiments, theory, and simulations, we establish how microjets emerging from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions may influence crystallization kinetics, opening new opportunities for the manufacture of crystalline materials.

papers.title: Soft material mechanical property degradation at high strain rates
papers.abstract: The rheometry of soft, tissue-like materials at ultra-high strain rates is critical to biomechanics, materials science, and medical engineering. One approach for characterizing high-rate material response is Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry (IMR), which infers viscoelastic constitutive behavior from the measured radius-time history of a laser-induced cavitation bubble. At these rates, materials may exhibit history-dependent behavior, including damage, fracture, and plasticity. However, conventional IMR analyses typically assume constant material properties throughout the cavitation event, limiting their ability to capture such changes. We present an IMR framework for identifying effective time varying material properties from measured cavitation radius histories. The framework allows the shear modulus, viscosity, or both to evolve during the event using normalized sigmoid histories. Synthetic tests recover prescribed constant and time varying material histories. Application to polyacrylamide and gelatin datasets yields effective material-property histories across formulations and experimental conditions. Viscosity decreased across the datasets, while the extent of shear modulus reduction varied with material and formulation. When both properties decreased, their reductions could occur at different stages of cavitation. This distinction in mechanical property degradation depends on both the property and its evolution during high-strain events.

papers.title: Elasto-inertial force exerted on a sphere oscillating in a fluid near a soft interface
papers.abstract: Fluid inertia can remain important in confined flows, even at low Reynolds number when convective inertia is negligible; yet its coupling with interface deformability is an open problem. Here, we theoretically investigate the high-frequency oscillations of an immersed sphere near an elastic wall in the lubrication regime. We first reconcile previous predictions for the added mass near a rigid wall by consistently matching the inner lubrication flow with the outer flow. Using this rigid-wall problem as a reference, we then develop a perturbative analysis of wall deformation and derive the leading elasto-inertial correction to the hydrodynamic force. Our results reveal that the coupling between interface softness and fluid inertia produces a dominant non-dissipative force contribution scaling as the power four of the frequency in the high-frequency limit, thus corresponding to the fourth time derivative of the sphere's position. This finding may have implications regarding the short-time dynamics of colloidal particles near deformable interfaces in biological and soft-matter settings.

papers.title: Complex nematic dynamics driven by steady Kolmogorov flows
papers.abstract: Complex nematohydrodynamics, including irregular defect dynamics, is commonly associated with time-dependent flows, most notably in active turbulence. Here we consider a simple model of a planar nematic subjected to a temporally steady but spatially varying flow and investigate the onset of time-dependent dynamics. Subjecting a passive nematic to steady Kolmogorov flow, while eliminating velocity fluctuations and hydrodynamic feedback, we find that increasing the flow strength drives a transition from stationary to periodic and, at stronger forcing, irregular spatiotemporal dynamics. The time-dependent states involve repeated local suppression of nematic order and director reorganisation, arising from the competition between spatially varying shear and nematic relaxation. Bifurcation and phase-space analyses characterise this progression, while reduced-order models identify the dynamical origins. A two-mode model captures the onset of periodic motion through a saddle-node infinite-period bifurcation. A five-mode Galerkin truncation further recovers the progression from stationary to periodic and irregular dynamics. These results allow us to explain how a fixed, spatially heterogeneous velocity field can generate temporal complexity through the nonlinear dynamics of nematic order alone.

papers.title: Sedimentation of flexible fibers through an ordered array of pillars
papers.abstract: In this study, we extend our previous work [Makanga \textit{et al.}, Physical Review Fluids 8, 044303 (2023)] to investigate the effects of a periodic array of pillars on the settling dynamics of a flexible fiber in a viscous fluid. By means of numerical simulations, we show that the fiber trajectory falls at long times into one of two migration modes, ``zigzag" and ``displacement", which are determined by the short-time scattering dynamics induced by fiber-pillar interactions. In the zigzag mode, there is no average displacement relative to the direction of gravity; the center of mass of the fiber follows a quasi-straight line. Conversely, in the displacement mode, there is a net displacement relative to the direction of gravity; the fiber center of mass follows a cyclical skew-bumping path. We show how this long-time behavior can be predicted using a theoretical model with minimal ingredients. These findings, together with the long-time transport properties of the fiber, provide insights into future experiments, as well as the design of gravity-based deterministic lateral displacement (DLD) devices to sort elongated particles based on their geometric and/or mechanical properties.

papers.title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
papers.abstract: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

papers.title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
papers.abstract: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.

papers.title: Viscous Gubser flow with conserved charges to benchmark fluid simulations
papers.abstract: We present semi-analytical solutions for the evolution of both the temperature and chemical potentials for viscous Gubser flow with conserved charges. Such a solution can be especially useful in testing numerical codes intended to simulate relativistic fluids with large chemical potentials. The freeze-out hypersurface profiles for constant energy density are calculated, along with the corresponding normal vectors and presented as a new unit test for numerical codes. We also compare the influence of the equation of state on the semi-analytical solutions. We benchmark the newly developed Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) code CCAKE that includes both shear viscosity and three conserved charges. The numerical solutions are in excellent agreement with the semi-analytical solution and also are able to accurately reproduce the hypersurface at freeze-out.

papers.title: Fragility of Aeolian Ripples
papers.abstract: Sand surfaces exposed to the wind are covered by aeolian sand waves of diverse wavelengths, from centimetres for small ripples to decameters for dunes. Sand dunes can be said to be antifragile, since their growth is not prohibited by storms, whereas ripples and megaripples are fragile since they get flattened. The fluid-entrainment hypothesis attributes their fragility to a common cause: the spontaneous aerodynamic entrainment of grains. Here, we challenge this conventional view by revealing its major shortcomings and inconsistencies. An alternative framework, routed in the granular bed rheology, posits that impact ripples are erased when the two-phase flow of ballistically hopping grains on a solid sand surface gives way to a three-phase flow, featuring an intermediate, collision-dominated, fluid-like transport layer. Notably, both martian wind-drag ripples and terrestrial aerodynamic ripples, which emerge via a hydrodynamic instability, are insensitive to such "surface-melting". Their destruction is predicated on the transition from aerodynamically smooth to rough conditions, instead. Our theoretical arguments are well supported by a stability diagram in terms of Shields number and grain diameter, assembled from a carefully reassessed large body of literature, and backed up by dedicated control measurements.

papers.title: Turbulent velocity statistics in convective boundary layers
papers.abstract: Large-eddy simulations (LES) of the convective atmospheric boundary layer (CBL) are used to investigate velocity variance statistics in turbulent sheared convection. The thirteen simulations span conditions from weak convection with longitudinal rolls to free penetrative convection with no mean wind. In the presence of thermal rolls, the near-surface streamwise variance profile exhibits an approximately logarithmic decay with a slope proportional to the friction velocity, $u_*$, and an added constant proportional to the convective velocity, $w_\star$. After the structural transition to convective cells, both the streamwise and spanwise variances follow the empirical stability and height dependencies of Wilson (\textit{Boundary-Layer Meteorol.}, 2008, vol. 129, pp. 353--369). The near-surface vertical (wall-normal) velocity variance is well described by Monin--Obukhov similarity with improved agreement using local-in-height scaling. Within the mixed layer, the peak vertical variance initially decreases relative to $w_\star$ as shear diminishes, before increasing and shifting downward as the flow approaches free convection. In contrast, the total turbulent energy decreases relative to $w_\star$ across the parameter space. The spanwise velocity variance represents the dominant turbulent component under weak convection and exceeds the streamwise variance throughout most of the convective regime. These statistical trends are attributed to the role of pressure, evaluated through variance budget contributions. Large-scale buoyancy production in the mixed layer is transported downward by pressure and redistributed preferentially to the spanwise component, coinciding with the presence of longitudinal roll motions. The weakening of this pressure-transport pathway for convective cells coincides with greater retention of vertical variance within the mixed layer.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical simulations of near resonant 2D soliton interaction in shallow water
papers.abstract: Experiments were carried out in {a} large wave basin ($27\times 30$\,m$^2$) to study the interactions of non-linear waves in shallow water (0.35\,m deep). A stereoscopic technique was used to measure the waves accurately over a vast area ($180$\,m$^2$). The numerical code {Tolosa-lct}, designed for simulating wave propagation in shallow water, reproduces the observations and extends the analysis for larger domains. The diffraction of oblique solitons is discussed. Mach interaction of two solitons occurs for some given incidence and amplitudes, producing a third soliton. A focus is made on the near resonant interaction of a soliton with a vertical wall. An example of a regular Mach interaction is shown, where a steady solution is achieved experimentally, with a maximum amplitude amplification of 3.2 at the wall.

papers.title: PQG-DL-Ekman: a triple-deck boundary layer theory for large-scale atmospheric flow with moist process closures
papers.abstract: Reduced mathematical models for atmospheric dynamics at various scales have a long and rich history. However, versions of such models that explicitly incorporate moisture and phase changes have been developed only fairly recently. This work merges one of said modeling innovations, namely Smith and Stechmann's \emph{precipitating quasigeostrophic} (PQG) model family, with a triple-deck boundary layer theory due to Klein et al.~that extends the classical QG-Ekman theory by an intermediate \emph{diabatic layer} (DL). A detailed analysis of the Clausius-Clapeyron relation and Kessler-type bulk microphysics closures is included in the systematic derivation of the resulting PQG-DL-Ekman theory. Furthermore, to illustrate some of the model's properties, explicit axisymmetric solutions of the precipitating diabatic layer equations are derived and combined with numerical sample solutions for the bulk flow.

papers.title: Sea Surface Roughness Dependence on Ocean Wave Parameters through Large Eddy Simulation with Local Subfilter Wave Drag
papers.abstract: Characterizing the Marine Atmospheric Boundary Layer (MABL) requires understanding the coupling between ocean waves and the turbulent atmospheric boundary layer above them. This coupling controls momentum exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean; it is of practical importance in the global climate, flow of ocean currents, ocean engineering, and offshore wind energy. Computational study of the MABL is complex because it must resolve the coupled physics of waves and turbulence over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This study expands on approaches for representing dynamic, local waves in Large Eddy Simulations (LES) of the MABL by developing a subfilter wave drag model to be local and scale-invariant. It explores the effects of different wave parameters (significant wave height and peak frequency of the wave energy spectrum) on the resulting momentum flux beyond monotonic relationships between surface stress through friction velocity $u_\ast$ and wind velocity above the surface $U_{10}$. Results are compared to field data and in a discussion on how representation of the MABL and associated momentum flux need to account for both wind and wave effects.

papers.title: Improving Airflow Network Models of Natural Ventilation: Geometry-Specific Pressures and Fluctuation Corrections
papers.abstract: Building energy models typically predict natural ventilation rates using airflow networks, which solve a system of orifice equations with exterior pressures as boundary conditions. This study investigates two improvements to these models: (i) geometry-specific exterior pressures obtained from large eddy simulations (LESs) and (ii) analytical corrections accounting for the nonlinear effects of pressure fluctuations on mean ventilation rates. We evaluate these improvements against coupled interior-exterior LESs of flows through 5824 windows, 2688 skylights, and 2752 interiors across idealized urban canopies. Replacing standard ASHRAE pressure coefficients with pressures from exterior-only LESs reduces the RMSE of predicted ventilation rates by approximately 50%, largely by capturing urban canopy flow effects that are poorly represented by standard shelter factors. Independently of the pressure source, mean-pressure airflow network predictions exhibit a nonlinear relationship with the LES ventilation rates. To address this discrepancy, we derive fluctuation corrections for mean-dominated and fluctuation-dominated flow regimes. These corrections eliminate the systematic nonlinearity and further reduce RMSE by 10-40% for most opening types and ventilation configurations. For windows, the combined improvements from geometry-specific surface pressures and fluctuation corrections increase the coefficient of determination $R^2$ from approximately 0.4 to 0.9. The results demonstrate the potential to accurately predict natural ventilation rates across different interior layouts while accounting for urban canopy effects and pressure fluctuations, using exterior-only LES pressure information.

papers.title: Comparison of the flamelet progress variable and thickened flame models for LES of turbulent combustion
papers.abstract: Large-eddy simulation (LES) of turbulent combustion requires closure models for unresolved flame structures and chemical processes. Two widely used but fundamentally different approaches are the flamelet/progress-variable approach (FPVA) and the dynamically thickened-flame model (TFM). Here, both are applied to methane-air combustion within a common numerical framework and evaluated for the Sandia D flame and a jet-in-crossflow representative of a non-assist waste-gas flare across a range of crosswind-to-jet velocity ratios. For the predominantly diffusion-controlled Sandia-D flame, FPVA and TFM exhibit similar accuracy, while FPVA is substantially less computationally expensive and converges faster under mesh refinement. More detailed chemical kinetics improve agreement with experimental measurements, with little additional cost for FPVA but a substantial increase for TFM. For the jet-in-crossflow, both approaches reproduce the experimentally observed reduction in combustion efficiency with increasing crosswind, but their predictions progressively diverge as the crosswind strength increases. This divergence coincides with the emergence of a locally premixed reaction branch captured by TFM but not represented by FPVA, whereas predictions in diffusion-dominated regions remain broadly similar. In TFM, the locally premixed branch is associated with elevated scalar dissipation and greater residual methane downstream, indicating that highly strained premixed combustion contributes to differences in predicted flare performance. These results show that FPVA and TFM can provide similar predictions in diffusion-dominated flames but differ substantially when crossflow induces locally premixed, highly strained combustion near the nozzle.

papers.title: Harmonic structure and parametric prediction of instantaneous power in oscillating foils
papers.abstract: A closed-form model is developed to predict the instantaneous lift, pitching moment, and power of an oscillating-foil energy harvester directly from its kinematic input. Such foils extract renewable power from moving water through sinusoidal heaving and pitching. However, due to their large-amplitude motion and vortex-dominated dynamics, classical unsteady aerodynamics cannot accurately predict the time-dependent force and power generation. To generate the model, 405 two-dimensional simulations are computed which vary heave amplitude, pitch amplitude, and frequency, representing the energy harvesting kinematic parameter space. The lift and pitching moment are decomposed into odd Fourier harmonics, and each Fourier coefficient is regressed on sixteen physics-based polynomial terms derived from the kinematic, power, and energy scalings. The regression is performed in two Ridge steps, one for attribution and one for the deployable predictor. The attribution shows that the first harmonic, which contains the mean power, depends on the motion amplitudes. The higher harmonics respond nonlinearly to the frequency, which determines the number and timing of the vortex shedding. The model recovers the cycle-averaged power with a leave-one-out $R^2$ of $0.98$, and reproduces the instantaneous lift with a median peak error of $9\%$ and a median phase error below $1\%$ of the period. The harmonic order of the response counts the discrete vortex events in each stroke, as confirmed by the wake visualization. The model's analytical expression for time-dependent force and power can be utilized as a fast and accurate alternative to high-fidelity simulations, specifically targeting device design and array optimization of oscillating foils.
